subject: physics_2
question_text: The electric lines of force do not intersect. Why?

verification.note: The 1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Physics-II paper the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. Hand-checked: the tangent to a line of force gives the direction of E; two intersecting lines would give two tangents, hence two directions of E at one point, which is impossible. Matches the book's answer (printed p.19).

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: A crossing gives two directions
steps.mark_note: Two tangents at the crossing point
lines: Suppose two electric lines of force
intersect at a point. The tangent to a line
of force at a point gives the direction of
the electric field there. At the crossing
point there would be two tangents, so two
directions of the electric field at one
steps.margin_note: First mark. Name the tangent rule — it is the link between the picture and the field direction.
steps.why: The argument is by contradiction: assume a crossing, apply the tangent rule to both lines, and the same point ends up with two field directions.
common_mistakes: Answering that the lines repel each other. Lines of force are a drawing, not objects that push.
Skipping the tangent rule and jumping to the conclusion. The two directions come FROM the two tangents.

recall.must_convey: That the tangent gives the field direction, so a crossing point would have two field directions.
accept: the tangent gives the direction of the field
reject: the field has only one direction

steps.memory_tip: Assume they cross, draw both tangents — the contradiction appears by itself.

steps.label: Two directions are impossible
lines: The electric field at a point can have only
one direction. Two directions at the same
point is impossible. Hence two electric

lines.text: One point has one field direction

steps.margin_note: Second mark. Close the contradiction: one point, one direction, so no crossing.
steps.why: E at a point is a single vector — the force on a unit positive charge there. A vector cannot point two ways at once, so the assumed crossing must be wrong.
common_mistakes: Writing not possible without saying WHAT is not possible — it is two field directions at one point.

recall.must_convey: That the field at a point has only one direction, so lines of force never intersect.
accept: the field cannot have two directions

steps.memory_tip: E is one vector at each point — one arrow, never two.

insider_note: Both marks live in the tangent argument — tangent gives direction, a crossing gives two, one point allows one.
